title: Carrying a bass by car and plane
summary: Stewart describes loading the bass head-first into the back seat, and buying a half-fare seat after flights broke the neck.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Now, what is the best way to put a bass in a car?

Well, I usually put my bass into our car, the one we have now, which is fairly big inside -- it's a four-door LTD. I put it in from the driver's side, the back seat — the back seat on the left hand driver's side of the car. I put the neck in first towards the front and gradually the bottom of the bass goes in and I put the bottom of the bass over the back seat near the window. It goes, you know, up near the window, and I think that's the best way that I can get it in by putting it in head-first, through the left hand side back seat.
Now, did you find over the years that it was very difficult traveling with the bass without it being damaged?

Well, yes, it was very difficult. Quite a few times, I flew, you know, I had to fly with my bass and of course, when I first started flying, I didn't have any better sense than to have them put it in the baggage compartment with all the rest of the baggage and paraphernalia and what have you and the way they handled the baggage was enough. I should have had better sense. A couple of times, my bass, when I went to get it, the neck was dangling, it was broken practically in half by the handling of it, which I finally wound up not doing what I first started out doing, having my bass put in the baggage and what have you. I bought a seat for my bass, so that it would be right alongside me and fortunately a seat would cost me half fare, which is better than nothing, you know.
That's right. And you should see me, ever since, I got wise to myself. I would have the seat right next to me with my baby right next to me, you know. That was it.
